C E L L U L A R T H E R A P I E S
Neutrophil antigen antibodies affect engraftment and
secondary graft failure in hematopoietic progenitor cell
transplantation

|
Sajjad Hassan
|
Herleen Rai
|

Department of Transfusion Medicine,

Abstract
Background: Research is limited on the role of antibodies against human
neutrophil antigen (HNA) in hematopoietic progenitor cell (HPC) transplanta-
tion outcomes.
Study Design and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on medi-
cal records of patients at the NIH Clinical Center enrolled in six research pro-
tocols. This case–control study included 21 patients tested for HNA antibodies
from January 2010 to March 2022 who underwent HPC transplantation. In
addition, 42 patients following the same research protocols were randomly
selected as a control group.
Results: The cumulative incidence of time to neutrophil engraftment was sig-
nificantly impacted by the patients' anti-HNA status (p = .042), with the
patients with anti-HNA experiencing delayed engraftment. Secondary graft
failure occurred in 4 out of 42 patients (9.52%; 95% confidence interval [CI]:
3.7–22.1) of the control group, while 5 out of 9 patients (55.5%; 95% CI: 26.7–
81.1) with anti-HNA experienced secondary graft failure (p = .005). Further-
more, patients with anti-HNA had a lower proportion (p = .008 for full and
p = .002 for partial chimerism) and cumulative incidence (p = .016 for full
and p = .010 for partial chimerism) of achieving donor chimerism compared
to the control group.
Discussion: The study reveals a potential link between anti-HNA and HPC
transplantation outcomes not previously reported. Patients with anti-HNA had
a lower proportion and cumulative incidence of achieving donor chimerism.
Additionally, anti-HNA status affected the time for neutrophil engraftment,
with a slower rate of neutrophil engraftment and increased risk of secondary
failure in patients with anti-HNA.

INTRODUCTION
Granulocytes are essential for the proper functioning of
the innate and adaptive immune systems, and the most
abundant component of these are neutrophils.1,2 Glyco-
proteins, known as human neutrophil antigens (HNA)
are expressed on the surface of human neutrophils. Five
systems of HNA are recognized with a total of 14 alleles.
Antibodies against HNA (anti-HNA) have been linked to
a range of pathophysiologies, including neonatal alloim-
mune neutropenia, autoimmune neutropenia, and trans-
fusion complications.3–7 Our understanding of the impact
of anti-HNA on hematopoietic progenitor cell (HPC)
transplantation outcomes is limited.
HPC transplantation is a common treatment for
hematological diseases and can restore hematological
function successfully. However, graft failure or poor graft
function are potential outcomes.8 While complications of
HPC transplantation, such as immune-mediated cytope-
nia, have been linked to anti-HNA, screening for anti-
HNA is usually performed in patients with unexplained
neutropenia before or after HPC transplantation.7,9–13
Only a limited number of studies have explored the
impact of anti-HNA on HPC transplantation. These stud-
ies primarily consist of individual case reports.3–5,14–16

While two clinical trials have investigated the association
between anti-HNA and HPC transplantation they have
not assessed donor chimerism.7,17 In this retrospective
case–control study, we examine primary and secondary
graft failure, graft function, and donor chimerism to gain
insights into the impact of anti-HNA on the outcomes of
HPC transplantation.
2
|
METHODS
2.1
|
Study cohort
Patients included in this study were admitted to the NIH,
Clinical Center between January 1, 2010, and March
31, 2022, under six institutional review board (IRB)
approved research protocols, which entailed written
informed consent (Supplementary Table 1). Data were
collected with IRB approval #000568 at the NIH. All
HPC transplant patients with anti-HNA and at least
10 months of follow-up were identified. Controls from
the same trials were randomly selected using a random
sampling method and matched at a 1:2 ratio. The list of
control subjects was generated using the NIH Clinical
Research Information System. Controls who did not
undergo stem cell transplantation or had a follow-up
period of less than 10 months were excluded and
replaced with another control. Since each protocol has
strict criteria for inclusion and exclusion based on demo-
graphics, clinical diagnosis, and clinical status, no further
matching was performed.
2.2
|
Anti-HNA detection
Anti-HNA was screened using the Granulocyte Immuno-
fluorescence Test (GIFT) and Granulocyte Agglutination
Test (GAT). If either test yielded a positive result, a screen-
ing test for HLA class I antibodies based on an Enzyme-
Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) is performed to rule
out false-positive screening. Antibody specificity was con-
firmed with the Monoclonal Antibody Immobilization of
Neutrophil Antigens Assay (MAINA). The assays were per-
formed as send-out tests (Neutrophil and Platelet Immu-
nology Laboratory, American Red Cross, St Paul, MN).
2.3
|
Donor chimerism assessment
Donor chimerism assessment was conducted using the
Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) Chimerism WBC test by
the Hematology service within the Department of Labo-
ratory Medicine at the NIH. The test employs PCR ampli-
fication of polymorphic STRs to identify donor-origin
myeloid cells and CD3+ T cells in the peripheral blood of
transplant recipients. Blood samples were collected in
ACDA or EDTA tubes, with a minimum WBC count of
0.5 �103/μL. Based on the quantified value of donor-
derived cells, the level of donor chimerism was assigned
as described in the Definitions section.
2.4
|
Definitions
Hematopoietic recovery, graft failure, poor graft function,
and donor chimerism were defined in accordance with
the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular
Therapy report.18
2.5
|
Statistical analysis
Data normality of independent sample groups was
assessed using the Shapiro-Wilks test, and variances were
compared with Levene's test.19 Depending on the appro-
priateness, two-sample comparisons were performed with
either the unpaired t-test or Mann–Whitney U test. Multi-
ple treatment groups were analyzed with either the para-
metric one-way analysis of variance or the nonparametric
Kruskal–Wallis Test. Correction for multiple compari-
sons was performed using either the Turkey test or the

RESULTS
This retrospective case–control study encompassed all
21 patients who were tested for anti-HNA in six clinical
trials involving HPC transplantation at NIH Clinical
Center. As controls, 42 patients in the same trials were
randomly selected (Supplementary Table 1).
3.1
|
Transplantation recipients
The demographics did not differ significantly between
the HNA-tested and control groups (Table 1). Out of the
group tested for HNA, 9 patients tested positive for anti-
HNA, while 12 tested negative. In the group with positive

anti-HNA results, 44% of patients exhibited antibody
specificity towards one or more specific neutrophil anti-
gens. One patient exhibited specificity against HNA-1a
(NA1), another against HNA-1b (NA2), one patient
showed anti-HNA specificity against both HNA-1a (NA1)
and HNA-1b (NA2), and one patient showed reactivity
with the CD18 integrin (Table 2).

3.2
|
Primary graft failure
Neutrophil recovery time was shorter in the control
group (median 16 days [range 12–27]) compared to the
positive anti-HNA group (median 20 days [range 13–54])
and the negative anti-HNA group (median 18.5 days
[range 11–53]) (Figure 1A). However, this difference was
not statistically significant (p = .14). The presence of
anti-HNA antibodies affected the proportions of patients
achieving neutrophil engraftment by day +30: 100% (95%
confidence interval [CI]: 91.6–100.0) in the control group,
77.7% (95% CI 45.2–96; p = .0282) in patients with posi-
tive anti-HNA, and 75% (95% CI 45.2–96.1; p = .0089) in
those with negative anti-HNA (Figure 1B). The cumula-
tive incidence of neutrophil engraftment in the positive
anti-HNA group was significantly lower than the control
group (p = .042), while no significant difference was
observed between the control and negative anti-HNA
groups (p = .25) (Figure 1C).
No statistical difference in median time, proportions,
or cumulative incidence of platelet recovery is observed
between the three groups (Supplementary Figure 1).

3.3
|
Secondary graft failure and poor
graft function
The number of patients who failed to maintain neutro-
phil engraftment after meeting recovery standards was
significantly higher for those with positive anti-HNA
compared to the control group (Figure 2). No significant
differences were seen in the proportion of patients receiv-
ing red blood cell transfusions between the control group
and the positive and negative anti-HNA groups (p = .17
and .59, respectively). Likewise, there were no significant
differences in the number of transfused units after
engraftment among the three groups (p = .08) (Supple-
mentary Table 2). Compared to the positive and negative
anti-HNA groups, the control group had fewer patients
receiving platelet transfusions (p = .27 & .02) and G-CSF
post-engraftment (p = .46 & .74). The mean post-engraft-
ment G-CSF dose in the control group was also lower
than in both the positive and negative anti-HNA groups,
but
this
difference
was
not
statistically
significant
(p = .15) (Table S3).
3.4
|
Donor chimerism
In the control group, 80.9% (95% CI 66.6–90.0) of the sub-
jects achieved full donor chimerism (Figure 3A). In con-
trast, the proportion of those achieving full donor
chimerism was 33.3% (95% CI 12.1–64.6; p = .008) in the
positive anti-HNA group and 75% (95% CI 46.7–91.1;
p = .69) in the negative anti-HNA group. The cumulative
incidence of achieving full donor chimerism was signifi-
cantly lower in the positive anti-HNA group compared to
the control group (p = .016), while no significant differ-
ence was observed between the control and negative anti-
HNA groups (p = .51) (3B).
In the control group, 97.6% (95% CI 87.7–99.9) of
patients achieved partial donor chimerism. In contrast,
55.5% (95% CI 26.7–81.1; p = .002) of patients with posi-
tive anti-HNA and 83.3% (95% CI 55.2–97.0; p = .12) of
patients with negative anti-HNA achieved partial donor
chimerism (Figure 3C). The cumulative incidence of
achieving partial donor chimerism was significantly
lower in the control group compared to the positive anti-
HNA group (p = .010), while no difference was observed
between the control and negative anti-HNA groups
(p = .32) (Figure 3D).
For myeloid engraftment, the proportion of engraft-
ment in the control group was 95.2% (95% CI 84.2–99.1),
compared to 44.4% (95% CI 18.8–73.3; p = .001) in
patients with positive anti-HNA and 83.3% (95% CI
55.2–97.0; p = .21) in those with negative anti-HNA
(Figure 4A). The control group had a significantly
higher cumulative incidence of myeloid chimerism com-
pared
to
the
positive
anti-HNA
group
(p = .003),
while no significant difference was observed between
the control and negative anti-HNA groups (p = .20)

(Figure 4B).
For lymphoid engraftment, the proportion of engraft-
ment in the control group was 80.9% (95% CI 66.7–90.0).
In contrast, patients with positive anti-HNA had a rate of
33.3% (95% CI 12.0–64.6; p = .008), and patients with
negative anti-HNA had a rate of 75.0% (95% CI 46.7–91.1;
p = .69) (Figure 4C). The positive anti-HNA group
showed a significantly lower cumulative incidence of
achieving lymphoid chimerism compared to the control
group (p = .012), while no difference was detected
between the control and negative anti-HNA groups
(p = .49) (Figure 4D).

DISCUSSION
Our study uncovers a potential link between anti-HNA
and HPC transplantation outcomes that have not been
reported before. Patients with positive anti-HNA had a
lower proportion and cumulative incidence of achieving
donor chimerism. Additionally, anti-HNA status affected
the time for neutrophil engraftment, with a slower rate of
neutrophil engraftment and increased risk of secondary
failure in patients with positive anti-HNA.
There have been several reports of neutropenia
following HPC transplantation in patients with anti-
HNA.4,7,10,17 Klumpp et al. reported a case of graft fail-
ure with profound neutropenia following HPC trans-
plantation
in
a
patient
with
anti-HNA
and
NA1
specificity.10 Stroncek et al. reported a case of graft fail-
ure prolonged neutropenia in a patient with high titers
anti-HNA and NB1 specificity.4 Tazzari et al. found
that within 60 days after HPC transplantation, 30 out
of 43 patients tested positive for anti-HNA. These
patients had decreased peripheral neutrophil levels for
up to 6 months post-transplantation.7 Klumpp et al.
conducted a prospective analysis showing that anti-
HNA
was
associated
with
delayed
neutrophil
engraftment.17
Our findings align with previous studies, supporting
the impact of anti-HNA on neutrophil engraftment.7,17
However, our study provides novel insights by applying a
competing risks framework and cumulative incidence
analysis.20 Thus we identified a statistically significant

difference in neutrophil recovery among patients with

ure 1). In addition, we integrated the findings with chi-
merism
studies
to
gain
a
more

Serial evaluation of a patient's chimerism status at
regular time intervals provides insights into engraftment
levels following HPC transplantation. Limited research
exists on the specific association between HNA anti-
bodies and chimerism.21 Our analysis shows that patients
with anti-HNA have lower rates of achieving full and
partial donor chimerism compared to the control group
(Figure 3). Although it is possible for a patient to have
successful hematopoietic recovery without full donor chi-
merism, as disease control can require varying amounts

of donor chimerism, our analysis showed that successful
hematopoietic recovery and achieving donor chimerism
are not always coinciding events. Although delayed, all
patients in our study with positive anti-HNA have even-
tually achieved hematopoietic recovery. However, only
33.3% and 55.5% achieved complete and partial donor
chimerism. This underscores the need for caution when
using hematopoietic recovery as an indicator of success-
ful HPC transplantation, particularly in patients with
HNA antibodies.
By day 100, 55% of positive anti-HNA patients were
only partially engrafted, with 44% achieving full mye-
loid and 33% full lymphoid chimerism (Figure 4). Partial
or mixed chimerism has been associated with an
increased risk of secondary graft failure in malignant

and non-malignant diseases, and this risk increases with
the degree of mixed chimerism.22–24 Our analysis also
revealed a higher incidence of secondary graft failure
and reliance on blood products in patients with positive
HNA antibodies. A statistically higher number of
patients with positive HNA antibodies failed to sustain
their neutrophil engraftment compared to those without
antibodies (Figure 2).
We examined G-CSF usage in our study, to determine
if it could have masked any potential poor graft function
after HPC transplantation (Table S3). While not reaching
statistical significance, a greater proportion of patients
with anti-HNA received G-CSF therapy and required a
higher average therapeutic dose than the control group.
G-CSF is commonly used to accelerate recovery from
neutropenia following a hematopoietic stem cell trans-
plantation.25 However, previous studies suggest that its
efficacy may be diminished in individuals with anti-HNA
as it stimulates the expression of HNA-2, which can
potentially decrease rather than increase neutrophil
levels, creating a negative feedback loop. These findings
suggest that G-CSF may not be as effective in mitigating
neutropenia in this specific patient population, resulting
in an elevated rate of secondary graft failure. Thus, fur-
ther research is warranted to explore its application in
this cohort of patients.14,26–28
In our study, among the 9 patients who tested positive
for
anti-HNA,
3
showed
HNA-1-specific
positivity
(Table 2). HNA-1 is a unique receptor present in neutro-
phils and basophils, also known as FCR-IIIb or CD16b,
with a low affinity.1 Contrary to previous findings,29 the
presence of HNA-1a (NA1) affected lymphoid engraft-
ment in one of the two patients positive for NA1-specific
antibodies in our study. This observation may be attrib-
uted to the anti-NA1 titers. Additionally, the HNA-1 sys-
tem exhibits diversity with four alleles, and individuals
can express anywhere from zero to four different HNA-1
alleles due to gene duplication and recombination.1 It is
important to note that without knowledge of the patient's
genotype and antibody titers, a definitive conclusion can-
not be reached, highlighting a limitation of our study and
emphasizing the significance of including them in rou-
tine clinical testing when ordering HNA screening
panels.
Although a relatively small number of patients were
analyzed in this study, we revealed that patients with
anti-HNA experienced delayed engraftment of neutro-
phils, a higher risk of secondary graft failure, and a
lower probability of achieving donor chimerism after
HPC transplantation. We recommend evaluating anti-
HNA status during HPC transplantation which would
allow us to better understand the impact of anti-HNA
and G-CSF therapy on transplantation outcomes in these
patients.
